title: Song of Solomon 8:8–14
context: The WEB assigns 8:8–9 to the Brothers, who ask what to do for their little sister and speak of a wall and a door; the Beloved answers that she is a wall and found peace in his eyes, and speaks of Solomon’s vineyard at Baal Hamon and her own vineyard. The Lover asks to hear her voice, and the Beloved closes the book by calling him to come away like a gazelle on the mountains of spices. The identity of the speakers and the meaning of the images in these verses are discussed, and both traditions read the close as shared ground on faithful love, with literal and allegorical readings held in both. Speaker names (Lover, Beloved, Friends, Brothers) follow the WEB headings, which are interpretive and are not part of the Hebrew text.

verses.text: We have a little sister. She has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister in the day when she is to be spoken for?
verses.arminianNotes:
The Brothers say, “We have a little sister... What shall we do for our sister in the day when she is to be spoken for?” Arminian readers note the brothers’ concern for their sister’s future.

Who the sister is, and how this relates to the Beloved, is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see family responsibility in the brothers’ question.

Shared ground: both traditions hedge the identity of the speakers and read the verse as care for one who is young, and allegorical readers have applied it to the church’s care for those not yet mature.

verses.text: If she is a wall, we will build on her a turret of silver. If she is a door, we will enclose her with boards of cedar.
verses.arminianNotes:
“If she is a wall, we will build on her a turret of silver. If she is a door, we will enclose her with boards of cedar.” Arminian readers note the contrast between a wall and a door, often taken as images of guarded or open conduct.

The exact meaning is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the brothers’ resolve to honor or protect her depending on her character.

Shared ground: both traditions hedge the images and read the verse as concern for honor and faithfulness.

verses.text: I am a wall, and my breasts like towers, then I was in his eyes like one who found peace.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Beloved answers, “I am a wall... then I was in his eyes like one who found peace.” Arminian readers note her confidence in her own faithfulness.

She speaks of finding peace in her beloved’s eyes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a statement of integrity and acceptance. The word “peace” may echo the name Solomon, though this is discussed.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as faithfulness rewarded with peace in love.

verses.text: Solomon had a vineyard at Baal Hamon. He leased out the vineyard to keepers. Each was to bring a thousand shekels of silver for its fruit.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Solomon had a vineyard at Baal Hamon. He leased out the vineyard to keepers.” Arminian readers note that the location of Baal Hamon is unknown.

The vineyard may stand for wealth or for a beloved person; the image is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hedge the meaning of Solomon’s vineyard and its keepers.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of a contrast between wealth and love, and they leave the relation of the Song to Solomon (1:1) as a question interpreters discuss.

verses.text: My own vineyard is before me. The thousand are for you, Solomon, two hundred for those who tend its fruit.
verses.arminianNotes:
“My own vineyard is before me. The thousand are for you, Solomon.” Arminian readers note that the WEB assigns this to the Beloved, who contrasts her own vineyard with Solomon’s.

Some readers assign the verse to the Lover instead.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hedge the speaker and the image.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as love freely given and not for sale, echoing 8:7, and allegorical readers have seen the believer’s life offered to God.

verses.text: You who dwell in the gardens, with friends in attendance, let me hear your voice!
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lover says, “You who dwell in the gardens, with friends in attendance, let me hear your voice!” Arminian readers note his desire to hear her speak.

The Song values the voice and words of both partners.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a longing for communication in love (cf. 2:14).

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as desire for fellowship, and allegorical readers hear God’s desire to hear the prayers of his people.

verses.text: Come away, my beloved! Be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices!
verses.arminianNotes:
The Beloved closes, “Come away, my beloved! Be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices!” Arminian readers note that the book ends with a call rather than a conclusion.

The image recalls 2:17.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see an open ending, and Christians reading allegorically have heard an echo of the church’s longing for Christ’s coming (cf. Rev 22:17, 20).

Shared ground: both traditions read the close as continuing love and longing, with literal and allegorical readings held side by side.
